Learning When to Abort in Transformer
Planning: A Mechanistic Study

Shi Feng   Qimin Zhong   Siwei Wang   Yifei Shen Affiliation: Harvard University  Shenzhen University    Shang-Hua Teng   Hao Liao   Wei Chen ††thanks: Corresponding author: Wei Chen, weic@microsoft.com. Affiliation: Harvard University  Shenzhen University Affiliation: Microsoft Research Asia  University of Southern California
Abstract

Planning does not by itself imply the ability to recognise errors, but recognising errors can improve planning capacity. In this paper, we study this phenomenon in Transformer planning. To analyze the inner mechanism, we follow the approach of Wang et al. (2024) and abstract planning as path-finding in graphs. In this setting, we train the model to detect the error of invalid transitions, i.e., after the model generates a next node that is not adjacent with the current node, the model should then generate a special abort token x. For expressiveness, we construct a Transformer with feed-forward width O⁡(|V|)O(|V|) for any fixed graph with node set VV. It can detect all possible invalid transitions, and select a valid next node if the prefix is valid. We then propose a worst-case lower bound on feed-forward width, which makes the detector’s linear width near-optimal up to logarithmic factors. In trained models, we demonstrate that invalid-transition detection increases previous-node attention, and most of the valid–invalid separation locates in the feed-forward network’s output. This accords with our theoretical insights. Finally, we use this error detection to improve the model’s performance: at inference, generating the abort token x will directly cause an external procedure to discard the attempt and restart from the original prompt. Experiments show that error detection combined with retry improves model’s planning reliability on graphs, Countdown, and mazes.

1 Introduction

Planning involves choosing a sequence of steps that leads from an initial state to a goal, and is ubiquitous in daily life. In recent years, Transformer-based large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for tasks requiring such multi-step planning, including mathematics and coding. Understanding how these models plan, and improving their planning capacity therefore becomes more and more important. In this paper, we study how learning to recognise invalid planning steps (or invalid transitions), could improve language-model planning. Traditional training on correct planning trajectories teaches a model which steps to take, but does not explicitly teach how to recognise invalid steps. In fact, planning ability does not need to bring failure recognition: a model may be able to find valid solutions yet fail to recognise that a problematic input contains invalid steps.

In human planning, however, failure recognition is also thought to play an important role in planning ability (Alexander and Brown, 2010; Fu et al., 2023).

Can a Transformer-based language model learn to detect invalid planning steps, what could be the underlying mechanism of this learning process, and how can this improve the model’s performance?

We conduct a mechanistic study on this problem, based on the path planning setup of ALPINE (Wang et al., 2024). In ALPINE, the planning task is abstracted as looking for valid paths in a fixed graph. The graph is not supplied as an input, hence the model must learn the graph’s structure from the training paths and find valid paths for unseen pairs. As for invalid planning steps, we focus on invalid transition, which is a step in the generated path from some node uu to node vv that has no corresponding edge in the underlying graph. To enable the Transformer to detect invalid transitions, we generate new training data containing valid path prefixes followed by an invalid transition, and then followed by a special abort token x. Only the abort token is supervised on these generated data, so that the Transformer could learn to flag invalid transitions without being trained to produce them. Intuitively, this is analogous to adding wrong planning steps and masking them in a planning task for the model to learn from mistakes.

Graph path-finding lets us distinguish two computations. Selecting the next node uses the current node’s outgoing edges and reachability to the target; detecting an invalid transition instead requires relating the previous node to the current one.

Learning from search traces and error markers can improve planning (Gandhi et al., 2024; Lehnert et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2026). Our focus is the mechanism: what computation invalid-transition detection requires, and whether abort supervision induces it in trained models. Theoretically, Proposition 1 of Section 4.1 shows that an additive score of the previous and current nodes with a threshold cannot detect arbitrary invalid transitions. In Section 4.2, we construct a one-layer Transformer that combines next-node selection with invalid-transition detection using the non-linear feed-forward layer with width linear in the number of nodes. The lower bound in Section 4.3 makes the detector’s linear width near-optimal up to logarithmic factors within the specified class of ReLU detectors. Empirically, Section 5 connects the abort decision to previous-node information and feed-forward network (FFN) processing in real trained Transformers. Attention measurements show whether the model looks back, interventions test whether previous-node information controls the abort decision, and direct logit attribution measures the FFN’s contribution to the abort signal. A fitted additive-logit alternative retains substantial detection error on the same supervised prefixes (Appendix B.2). These findings are consistent with the computational dependencies identified by the theory.

We then ask whether the learned signal improves planning. At inference, a harness, an external procedure surrounding the model, discards an attempt when x is emitted and restarts from the original prompt. Experiments on random graphs, Countdown and mazes show that this procedure improves planning reliability (Section 6). Unlike verifier-ranked best-of-NN sampling (Cobbe et al., 2021; Lightman et al., 2024), it does not require a fixed set of complete candidates or a separate correctness verifier: the model supplies the signal for restarting an attempt.

Our contributions are threefold: a simple training method that turns local errors into abort supervision; a mechanistic account of invalid-transition detection, combining a one-layer Transformer construction, a capacity lower bound and experiments on trained models; and an inference-time restart harness that uses the learned signal to improve planning across tasks and models.

2 Related Work

Our mechanistic starting point is ALPINE (Wang et al., 2024), which explains how Transformers select the next node using adjacency and reachability information. We build on this account to study invalid-transition detection. Complementary work studies how models compose reachability information to select future steps (Zhong et al., 2025), represent and maintain the current planning state during search (Phua et al., 2026), and improve planning through reinforcement-learning fine-tuning (Wang et al., 2026).

Our training approach belongs to the line of work on learning from search and error traces. Gandhi et al. (2024) train on complete search trajectories containing exploratory mistakes and backtracking, while Lehnert et al. (2024) train models to imitate A∗ search dynamics. Closer to our setting, Huang et al. (2025) train on erroneous actions followed by in-context corrections. Their models recognise mistakes, but self-correction does not improve plan validity in their evaluation. We instead separate detection from recovery: the model learns to flag an invalid transition, and an external procedure handles retry.

Self-Backtracking (Yang et al., 2026) is the closest method. It learns a token that triggers rollback and further search from an earlier state; our harness restarts from the original prompt. Its error-example loss supervises both the correct prefix and the backtrack token, whereas ours supervises only the abort token. Our labels require checking one transition, rather than determining that a prefix admits no valid completion, which can require searching over future continuations (Bylander, 1994). In our small-model Countdown experiments, we cross the two objectives with restart and rollback decoders. Abort-only supervision performs better with either decoder, suggesting that the simpler objective contributes to the gain in this setting (Appendix B.4). Our mechanistic analysis further distinguishes this work by combining an explicit Transformer construction with experiments on the learned computation.

Additionally, some work uses separate signals to guide generation. State–action verifiers (Arora and Kambhampati, 2023) check whether an action is valid in the current state. Process-verifier approaches use information about whether a prefix admits a valid completion (Botta et al., 2025), or learned estimates of the quality of partial generations (Rohatgi et al., 2026), to guide sampling and backtracking. In our approach, the planner itself (rather than an independent verifier) learns to emit the abort signal during generation. Confidence-token methods (Chuang et al., 2024) are also related, but estimate the reliability of the overall answer rather than whether the latest step is invalid.

3.2 Path-Planning Task, Data, and Training

We follow the graph path-finding setup of ALPINE (Wang et al., 2024). Fix a directed acyclic graph (DAG) G=(V,E)G=(V,E) with n=|V|n=|V| nodes. Given a source ss and a reachable target tt, the model receives the prompt s t and needs to generate a node sequence starting at ss, ending at tt, and following graph edges. We define a valid path prefix as a node sequence that starts at ss and follows only graph edges, and write u↝tu\rightsquigarrow t when uu can reach tt, including t↝tt\rightsquigarrow t.

There are two types of training trajectories. Correct training trajectories have the form s t s u1u_{1} … t, where s u1u_{1} … t is a valid path from ss to tt. These trajectories are used to train the usual sequence generation process, and thus receive the usual next-token loss. Error trajectories add supervision about invalid transitions. Each contains a valid prefix followed by one non-edge p→ip\to i and the token x. Only the final x is supervised; the prefix and invalid transition provide context, not prediction targets. We call this training signal abort supervision. We call the resulting model a +x+\texttt{x} model, and a model trained only on correct trajectories the baseline. The detailed loss formulation is given in (11) (Appendix B.1).

Our abort labels are local: in graph planning, determining whether a transition p→ip\to i is invalid only requires checking whether (p,i)∈E(p,i)\in E, without reasoning about whether the current prefix can still reach the target. Thus, constructing error trajectories requires only a local edge check, rather than solving the remaining planning problem.

For graph experiments, each edge i→ji\to j with i<ji<j is included independently with probability 0.10.1. Reachable source–target pairs are randomly split into training and test sets, except that direct-edge pairs always enter training. Each training pair contributes 2020 valid paths. The +x+\texttt{x} dataset adds one error trajectory per correct trajectory, and minibatches sample uniformly from this mixture. The loss averages over supervised tokens: correct trajectories supply multiple labels, error trajectories only one. Thus, correct trajectories make up half the batch on average but supply most labels.

We denote an architecture by layer count/head count/embedding size and compare 1/1/1201/1/120, 1/2/1201/2/120 and 1/2/3841/2/384. All use feed-forward width r=4​dr=4d, where dd is embedding size. The experiments use GELUs (Gaussian error linear units), layer normalisation and tied embedding/unembedding weights. Models are trained for 10410^{4} updates with batch size 1,0241{,}024 and learning rate 5×10−45\times 10^{-4}; Appendix B.1 gives the full protocol. Graph results use five seeds, each with an independently generated graph. Error bars are standard errors (s.e.) over seeds and gains are paired.

4 Theory of Invalid-Transition Detection in Path-Planning

Let A(p,i)true=𝟏[(p,i)∈E]A^{\mathrm{true}}_{(p,i)}=\mathbf{1}[(p,i)\in E] be the graph’s adjacency matrix, where 𝟏​[⋅]\mathbf{1}[\cdot] is 11 when its condition holds and 00 otherwise. The true reachability matrix has entry R(t,u)true=𝟏[u↝t]R^{\mathrm{true}}_{(t,u)}=\mathbf{1}[u\rightsquigarrow t].

4.1 Additive Detection Is Insufficient

To output the abort token correctly, the model needs to determine whether the most recent transition p→ip\to i is valid, that is, whether (p,i)∈E(p,i)\in E. We next show that simply adding separate functions of pp and ii in a single thresholded score is not sufficient for general graphs.

Proposition 1.

If AtrueA^{\mathrm{true}} has nodes p≠p′p\neq p^{\prime} and i≠i′i\neq i^{\prime} with A(p,i)true=A(p′,i′)true=1A^{\mathrm{true}}_{(p,i)}=A^{\mathrm{true}}_{(p^{\prime},i^{\prime})}=1 and A(p,i′)true=A(p′,i)true=0A^{\mathrm{true}}_{(p,i^{\prime})}=A^{\mathrm{true}}_{(p^{\prime},i)}=0, then no threshold on an additive function f⁡(p)+g⁡(i)f(p)+g(i) can correctly classify all four transitions as edges or non-edges, whether larger scores indicate validity or invalidity.

To see why, consider the two edges (p,i)(p,i) and (p′,i′)(p^{\prime},i^{\prime}), whose crossed pairs (p,i′)(p,i^{\prime}) and (p′,i)(p^{\prime},i) are non-edges. For an additive function ϕ⁡(p,i)=f⁡(p)+g⁡(i)\phi(p,i)=f(p)+g(i), with f,g:V→ℝf,g:V\to\mathbb{R},

ϕ⁡(p,i)+ϕ⁡(p′,i′)=ϕ⁡(p,i′)+ϕ⁡(p′,i).\phi(p,i)+\phi(p^{\prime},i^{\prime})=\phi(p,i^{\prime})+\phi(p^{\prime},i).

Thus, the two edge scores and the two non-edge scores have the same total, so no threshold can place both edges on one side and both non-edges on the other.

Thus, general invalid-transition detection with a scalar threshold requires a non-additive combination of previous-node and current-node information. In the next subsection, we show how a Transformer implements this check by selecting the current node’s entry from the previous node’s adjacency row.

4.2 A Gated Lookup for Invalid Transition Detection

In this subsection, we construct a one-layer, two-head Transformer that performs path planning and invalid-transition detection simultaneously. We consider input sequences of the form “s​t​s​u1​…​uks\ t\ s\ u_{1}\dots u_{k}”, where s↝ts\rightsquigarrow t.

Theorem 2.

Given a DAG GG with adjacency matrix AtrueA^{\mathrm{true}} and reachability matrix RtrueR^{\mathrm{true}}, for every ε>0\varepsilon>0 there is a 11-layer, 22-head Transformer with embedding size O⁡(|V|)O(|V|) and feed-forward width O⁡(|V|)O(|V|) that, for every input sequence “s​t​s​u1​…​uks\ t\ s\ u_{1}\dots u_{k}” for which (u0,…,uk−1)(u_{0},\dots,u_{k-1}) is a valid path prefix, where u0=su_{0}=s, k≥1k\geq 1, and uk≠tu_{k}\neq t, generates with probability at least 1−ε1-\varepsilon

  1. (i)

    the token x, if A(uk−1,uk)true=0A^{\mathrm{true}}_{(u_{k-1},\,u_{k})}=0, and

  2. (ii)

    otherwise a node uk+1u_{k+1} that is both an out-neighbour of uku_{k} and able to reach tt, whenever such a node exists.

Write p=uk−1p=u_{k-1} and i=uki=u_{k} for the previous and current nodes. One attention head retrieves the target’s reachability row Rtrue(t,:)R^{\mathrm{true}}_{(t,:)}; the other retrieves the previous node’s adjacency row Atrue(p,:)A^{\mathrm{true}}_{(p,:)}. The residual connection retains the current node’s one-hot vector eie_{i}. Thus, at exact attention the relevant FFN input blocks are Rtrue(t,:)⊕Atrue(p,:)⊕eiR^{\mathrm{true}}_{(t,:)}\oplus A^{\mathrm{true}}_{(p,:)}\oplus e_{i}, where ⊕\oplus denotes concatenation.

The FFN’s first linear map reads the current node’s adjacency row Atrue(i,:)A^{\mathrm{true}}_{(i,:)} from eie_{i}, and thus the parameter becomes Rtrue(t,:)⊕Atrue(p,:)⊕ei⊕Atrue(i,:)R^{\mathrm{true}}_{(t,:)}\oplus A^{\mathrm{true}}_{(p,:)}\oplus e_{i}\oplus A^{\mathrm{true}}_{(i,:)}. Its first |V||V| ReLU units use Rtrue(t,:)R^{\mathrm{true}}_{(t,:)} and Atrue(i,:)A^{\mathrm{true}}_{(i,:)}, compute max⁡(0,R(t,v)true+A(i,v)true)=R(t,v)true+A(i,v)true\max(0,R^{\mathrm{true}}_{(t,v)}+A^{\mathrm{true}}_{(i,v)})=R^{\mathrm{true}}_{(t,v)}+A^{\mathrm{true}}_{(i,v)}, selecting out-neighbours of ii that can reach tt (if such nodes exist), as in the adjacency–reachability account of Wang et al. (2024). The other |V||V| units combine Atrue(p,:)A^{\mathrm{true}}_{(p,:)} with eie_{i} to check the preceding transition. For each node vv, a unit computes

max(0,𝟏[i=v]+A(p,v)true−1)=𝟏[i=v]A(p,v)true.\max\big(0,\mathbf{1}[i=v]+A^{\mathrm{true}}_{(p,v)}-1\big)=\mathbf{1}[i=v]\,A^{\mathrm{true}}_{(p,v)}. (2)

Their output suppresses the abort logit when the preceding transition is valid (when the sum of detection units is 1), and otherwise do nothing, letting the abort logit be largest (when the sum of detection units is 0).

The detector uses |V||V| units, while the complete FFN has width 2​|V|2|V|. Appendix A.1 gives the detailed architecture and weights and shows that the logit separation persists with finite attention scores.

Remark 1 (Observed reachability and retry).

Let R(t,u)obs=1R^{\mathrm{obs}}_{(t,u)}=1 when a training path ending at tt contains uu. Using RobsR^{\mathrm{obs}} instead of RtrueR^{\mathrm{true}} can affect next-node selection, but not invalid-transition detection. With exact checks of every transition (including the final one) and both endpoints, every accepted path is valid without a global ground-truth check. If independent, length-bounded attempts each succeed with fixed probability π>0\pi>0, retry succeeds within KK attempts with probability 1−(1−π)K1-(1-\pi)^{K} and terminates almost surely without a fixed budget. Thus, retry can overcome incomplete observed reachability (Wang et al., 2024).

4.3 How Much Capacity Does the Detector Require?

Suppose that the previous node pp, current node ii, and target node tt are represented at the FFN input by separate one-hot blocks, i.e., xp,i,t=ep⊕ei⊕etx_{p,i,t}=e_{p}\oplus e_{i}\oplus e_{t}. A width-rr ReLU FFN computes FFN⁡(x)=ReLU⁡(x​W1+b1)​W2+b2\mathrm{FFN}(x)=\mathrm{ReLU}(xW_{1}+b_{1})W_{2}+b_{2}. Let W1(p),W1(i),W1(t)∈ℝn×rW_{1}^{(p)},W_{1}^{(i)},W_{1}^{(t)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r} be the row blocks of W1W_{1} acting on the three node inputs. The hh-th FFN unit receives

W1(p)​[p,h]+W1(i)​[i,h]+W1(t)​[t,h]+b1​[h].W_{1}^{(p)}[p,h]+W_{1}^{(i)}[i,h]+W_{1}^{(t)}[t,h]+b_{1}[h].

The FFN’s contribution to the abort logit is

zxFFN(p,i,t)=(ReLU(xp,i,tW1+b1)W2+b2)WU[:,x].\displaystyle z_{\texttt{x}}^{\mathrm{FFN}}(p,i,t)=\bigl(\mathrm{ReLU}(x_{p,i,t}W_{1}+b_{1})W_{2}+b_{2}\bigr)W^{U}[:,\texttt{x}]. (3)

Since transition validity depends only on (p,i)(p,i), we can fix any target t0t_{0}. Then W1(t)[t0,:]W_{1}^{(t)}[t_{0},:] is constant and can be absorbed into b1b_{1}. Thus, for a fixed target, invalid-transition detection reduces to a width-rr ReLU network over the previous and current nodes.

Theorem 3.

Suppose that a width-rr one-hidden-layer ReLU FFN receives the previous node pp, current node ii, and target tt as the input ep⊕ei⊕ete_{p}\oplus e_{i}\oplus e_{t}. If, for every DAG on |V||V| nodes, there exist FFN parameters for which the sign of zxFFN​(p,i,t)z_{\texttt{x}}^{\mathrm{FFN}}(p,i,t) correctly determines whether (p,i)∈E(p,i)\in E for every p,i,t∈Vp,i,t\in V, then

r=Ω⁡(|V|log2⁡|V|).r=\Omega\left(\frac{|V|}{\log^{2}|V|}\right).

To prove the theorem, we bound the number of adjacency matrices representable by a width-rr network using the VC dimension of piecewise-linear networks (Bartlett et al., 2019) and the Sauer–Shelah lemma, and compare it with the 2(|V|2)2^{\binom{|V|}{2}} DAGs obtained by choosing arbitrary forward edges under a fixed node ordering (Appendix A.2). The detector in Theorem 2 uses |V||V| ReLU units, matching this worst-case lower bound up to logarithmic factors in this class.

5 Mechanistic Analysis of Abort Supervision

In this section, we examine whether trained models implement the invalid-transition detection mechanism suggested by our theoretical analysis. We study previous-node attention and its causal role in the abort decision, then use direct logit attribution (DLA) to locate the abort signal. Additional analyses of learned adjacency and reachability representations are in Appendix B.2. We compare baseline and +x+\texttt{x} models with the 1/2/120 and 1/2/384 architectures. For each graph size and architecture, we train both conditions from scratch on five independently generated graphs (Section 3).

At the beginning, we check that these models can both find valid paths and recognise failures. The 1/2/384 +x+\texttt{x} models produce a valid path in more than 90%90\% of single draws at every tested graph size, averaging over the five graphs at each size (Figure 3a). Their abort precision, the fraction of emitted aborts whose prefixes admit no valid completion, is 9494–99%99\% across these sizes (Appendix B.1). For the causal interventions and DLA, we use six independently generated n=300n=300 graphs, each with a trained 1/2/384 +x+\texttt{x} model. On held-out prefixes with an injected invalid transition, these models assign a mean probability of 99.7%99.7\% to the abort token (Appendix B.2). This strong abort response gives us a clear setting in which to study how the decision is made.

5.1 Previous-Node Information Drives the Abort Decision

We first test whether abort supervision increases attention to the previous node. For each model, we feed 3,000 correct held-out paths as fixed input sequences and average the attention weights over the two heads and over sequences containing each position. We measure attention on the previous node (key q−1q-1) and the mean attention on the other intermediate emitted nodes (keys 3,…,q−23,\ldots,q-2). We average each quantity over q=5,…,8q=5,\ldots,8, where this comparison set is nonempty, and take their ratio. A ratio of 11 means that the previous node receives the same attention as an average intermediate node. This ratio rises from 0.88 to 2.52 at d=384d=384 (Figure 2), with an average paired increase of 1.65±0.091.65\pm 0.09 over five seeds and five graph sizes. At d=120d=120, the corresponding increase is 0.39±0.250.39\pm 0.25.

The above measurement uses only correct paths and therefore captures the model’s general tendency to look back. We then test whether attention depends on transition validity. On six n=300n=300 graphs, the head with larger previous-node attention on injected invalid prefixes assigns 0.58 attention mass to the previous node after an invalid transition, compared with 0.17 after a valid transition.

We next test whether previous-node information causally affects the abort decision. We use the six n=300n=300, 1/2/384 +x+\texttt{x} models described above. For each graph, we take 2,000 held-out correct paths, cut each path at a random interior node uku_{k}, and append a node ww that is not a successor of uku_{k}. This produces an invalid prefix “s​t​u0​…​uk​ws\ t\ u_{0}\ldots u_{k}\ w”, and we measure P⁡(x)P(\texttt{x}) at the position immediately after ww. We retain prefixes for which a previous-node replacement can make both adjacent transitions valid, so the interventions use the same set of prefixes.

Table 2 reports interventions on the subset of prefixes for which ww can still reach the target. For each graph, we call the head with more attention to the previous node on invalid prefixes the main head. Removing its attention to the previous node and renormalising lowers P⁡(x)P(\texttt{x}) from 0.990.99 to 0.090.09, while removing previous-node attention from both heads lowers it to 0.0080.008. We also change only the previous node. Specifically, we replace uku_{k} by a node p′p^{\prime} such that (uk−1,p′)∈E(u_{k-1},p^{\prime})\in E and (p′,w)∈E(p^{\prime},w)\in E. The resulting prefix is valid and differs from the injected-invalid prefix only at the previous-node position. This change lowers P⁡(x)P(\texttt{x}) to 0.0010.001. Finally, we set the FFN output at the final position to zero before the residual addition, and then apply the final layer normalisation and unembedding as usual. This totally removes the abort response.

All rows of Table 2 are restricted to prefixes whose injected node ww can still reach the target. This avoids mixing invalid-transition detection with dead-end detection: after the previous-node swap, the prefix is valid and the target is still reachable, so the model no longer has a reason to abort. Appendix B.2 gives the full protocol, controls, and uncertainty estimates.

5.2 Direct Logit Attribution Locates the Abort Signal in the FFN

The interventions above show that previous-node information causally affects the abort decision. We next take a closer look at where this information is converted into an abort signal, using direct logit attribution (DLA). Let XX be the sum of token and positional embeddings. For our one-layer Transformer, the residual stream before the final normalisation is

H=X+MHA⁡(LN1⁡(X))+FFN⁡(LN2⁡(X+MHA⁡(LN1⁡(X)))).H=X+\operatorname{MHA}\bigl(\operatorname{LN}_{1}(X)\bigr)+\operatorname{FFN}\!\left(\operatorname{LN}_{2}\!\left(X+\operatorname{MHA}\bigl(\operatorname{LN}_{1}(X)\bigr)\right)\right).

The first two terms contain the information retrieved by attention, while the last term is the output after this information passes through the nonlinear FFN. Here LN1\operatorname{LN}_{1} and LN2\operatorname{LN}_{2} are the layer normalisations before attention and before the FFN, respectively.

DLA measures how much each part directly contributes to the abort logit in the same forward pass. For example, let MM denote the FFN output. Its contribution is zxM=wx⊤​[g⊙(M−mean⁡(M))/std⁡(H)]z_{\texttt{x}}^{M}=w_{\texttt{x}}^{\top}[g\odot(M-\operatorname{mean}(M))/\operatorname{std}(H)]. All quantities here are evaluated at the final position: wxw_{\texttt{x}} is the abort unembedding vector, gg is the final layer-normalisation scale vector, and std⁡(H)\operatorname{std}(H) includes the numerical stabiliser. Intuitively, this is the amount of abort logit that disappears if the FFN contribution is set to zero. It is an attribution, rather than rerunning the model with the FFN removed. We similarly compute the contribution before the FFN. Comparing these contributions between valid and invalid prefixes (as described in the last subsection) shows whether most of the valid–invalid separation is already written directly before the FFN or instead appears in the FFN output.

On target-reachable invalid prefixes, the direct contribution before the FFN changes little when the previous node is swapped to make the last transition valid (−0.68-0.68 to −1.15-1.15), while the FFN contribution drops from +29.6+29.6 to +1.5+1.5; the total abort logit falls from 29.029.0 to 0.30.3. Thus, little of the valid–invalid difference is written directly into the abort logit before the FFN; most of it appears in the FFN output. The same pattern holds for the abort margin, defined as the abort logit minus the largest node logit: the pre-FFN contribution changes from −1.0-1.0 to −1.7-1.7, while the FFN contribution changes from +22.4+22.4 to −10.2-10.2. Since the FFN receives only the pre-FFN residual stream, the information needed to distinguish the two prefixes must already be present there, but it is the FFN transforms it into a strong abort-versus-continue signal. This accords with our analysis, i.e., an additive score is not enough (X+MHA⁡(LN1⁡(X))X+\operatorname{MHA}\bigl(\operatorname{LN}_{1}(X)\bigr)), and the ReLU in FFN layer is critical for the abort signal. Appendix B.2 gives the full decomposition, including the unit-level analysis.

6 Planning with the Learned Abort Signal

We now ask whether the learned abort signal improves planning. We evaluate graphs, Countdown, and mazes; Countdown and maze experiments use 1/2/3841/2/384 models. All models are trained for 10410^{4} updates with batch size 1,0241{,}024 and learning rate 5×10−45\times 10^{-4}. As in Section 3, correct trajectories receive standard next-token supervision, while error trajectories supervise only the final abort token. All results use sampling at temperature 11.

We use a simple restart harness with draw budget KK. If the +x+\texttt{x} model emits x, the current draw is rejected and generation restarts from the original prompt. Otherwise, the completed output is checked by a domain-specific acceptance test 𝒜\mathcal{A}, which provides a second reason to reject a draw without checking full correctness. In graphs, 𝒜\mathcal{A} requires at least two path-node tokens and a final node equal to the target, but does not check intermediate edges. In Countdown, it requires a nonempty, well-formed sequence of equations whose last stated result equals the target, without checking arithmetic or operand availability. In mazes, it accepts every non-aborting output. After any rejection, the model draws again until an output is accepted or the budget KK is exhausted. The baseline uses the same acceptance rule and budget, but has no learned abort signal.

We report three metrics: single-shot validity is the valid-output rate of one draw; harness validity is the rate at which the harness returns a valid output, counting exhausted budgets as failures; and mean draw count is averaged over all evaluation instances, with an exhausted budget counted as KK draws (Appendix B.1).

6.1 Graph Path-Finding

Abort supervision can reduce single-shot validity, especially at smaller model size: at n=500n=500, the two d=120d=120 models lose about 1111 percentage points, whereas the loss for d=384d=384 is at most 2.82.8 points across the tested sizes. With retry, however, the +x+\texttt{x} model has higher harness validity than the baseline at every graph size for d=384d=384 (Figure 3b), reaching 98.998.9–99.7%99.7\% compared with 95.095.0–98.3%98.3\%. This gain requires only a small number of additional draws: averaged over all instances, the +x+\texttt{x} harness uses 1.031.03–1.091.09 draws per instance, compared with 1.011.01 for the baseline, an increase of only 0.020.02–0.080.08 draws (Figure 3d) in expectation.

Figure 3c shows how the learned abort signal changes the composition of invalid outputs. In a single draw, many errors that would otherwise appear as non-edge or wrong-end outputs are replaced by aborts. The harness then rejects these aborting draws and resamples, so many of these errors disappear from the returned output: the rate of returned outputs with an invalid transition falls from 2.4%2.4\% for the baseline to 0.4%0.4\% for +x+\texttt{x} at d=384d=384, and from 5.4%5.4\% to 3.6%3.6\% at d=120d=120. The gain persists when we match correct-trajectory exposure by doubling +x+\texttt{x} training updates (Appendix B.3).

6.2 Countdown

In this dataset, three numbers must be combined with +,−,×,÷+\,,-\,,\times\,,\div to reach a target. Intermediate values and targets are restricted to 11–100100. We enumerate all three-number multisets over 11–2020 together with all targets reachable under these restrictions, giving 16,11716{,}117 distinct instances, and hold out a disjoint tenth. A valid solution writes one equation per operation, a op b = c: the two operands are removed from the available numbers and the result is inserted. Every operation must be correct, and the final result must equal the target.

To construct an error trajectory, we corrupt the result after one =. For each trajectory, we choose one of two corruption types with equal probability: either adding or subtracting a small offset of magnitude 11–33, or replacing the result with a random value. Random replacements often produce obviously implausible results, whereas small offsets produce plausible-looking arithmetic errors that require checking the operation more carefully. Mixing the two reduces the chance that the model learns a shortcut based only on unusually large or small results. The corrupted equation is the invalid transition and is followed immediately by x; only this final x receives loss on the error trajectory. We denote by ρ\rho the ratio of error trajectories to correct trajectories.

At ρ=1\rho=1, the +x+\texttt{x} model improves harness validity by +8.2±0.9\mathbf{+8.2\pm 0.9} percentage points (Figure 4). This comes at a higher sampling cost: averaged over all instances, the +x+\texttt{x} harness uses 3.73.7 draws per instance, counting an exhausted budget of 100100 in full, compared with 1.11.1 for the baseline. The +x+\texttt{x} harness fails on 51%51\% of instances: it returns an output with incorrect arithmetic on 26%26\% and one using an unavailable number on 24%24\%, and it exhausts its budget without accepting an output on 1.2%1.2\%. The baseline harness fails on 59%59\% of instances (Figure 4c).

We next vary the amount of abort supervision. Averaging repeated baseline runs within each seed gives a harness validity of 41.3±0.7%41.3\pm 0.7\% over five seeds. The gain from +x+\texttt{x} increases monotonically from +2.2±0.6+2.2\pm 0.6 percentage points at ρ=0.25\rho=0.25 to +11.6±1.3+11.6\pm 1.3 points at ρ=4\rho=4 (Figure 4b). Abort supervision also improves single-shot validity, by 3.0±0.53.0\pm 0.5 percentage points at ρ=1\rho=1 and 4.7±0.84.7\pm 0.8 points at ρ=4\rho=4 (Figure 4a). This differs from the graph setting, where most of the harness gain comes from retrying after an abort. On Countdown, validity improves even before retry, suggesting that abort supervision may also improve representations used to generate valid equations.

6.3 Mazes

In a 10×1010\times 10 maze with random walls, the model starts facing East and emits relative-direction tokens: F moves forward, L and R turn left and right, and T turns around. Each token changes direction as needed and then advances one cell. For each of four independently generated mazes, we split reachable source–target pairs between training and test sets with probability 0.50.5 each. Training uses correct paths and an equal number of error trajectories.

A valid output reaches the target without crossing a wall. Error trajectories contain one wall-crossing move followed by the supervised abort token. For mazes, the acceptance test 𝒜\mathcal{A} accepts every non-aborting output. Thus, the harness retries only when the model emits x; wall crossings are checked only offline when computing validity.

Rejecting outputs that contain x and drawing again improves harness validity by +9.3±0.9\mathbf{+9.3\pm 0.9} percentage points (Figure 5). This requires 1.701.70 draws per instance on average for the +x+\texttt{x} harness, while the baseline always accepts its first draw. In single-shot generation, abort supervision reduces the wall-crossing rate from 22.5%22.5\% to 9.4%9.4\%, with some of these failures replaced by aborts. The harness retries aborting draws, reducing wall crossings in returned outputs from 22.5%22.5\% for the baseline to 13.7%13.7\% for +x+\texttt{x}. Wrong-end errors remain at 2020–23%23\%: neither the learned abort signal nor the acceptance test detects them (Figure 5a).

7 Conclusion

Error trajectories can teach a Transformer to detect invalid transitions by supervising only a final abort token. Our theoretical analysis characterises the required previous–current interaction and gives a one-layer construction in which attention retrieves information and the FFN checks transition validity. The width lower bound further characterises the capacity required within the specified readout class. In trained models, abort supervision increases previous-node attention, and the FFN produces most of the validity-dependent abort signal. Using this learned signal to reject and retry improves planning reliability on graphs, Countdown and mazes.

AI use statement

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools were used to assist with parts of the research and writing process. Claude (Anthropic) was used for code debugging and as an aid in literature search, while Claude and Codex (OpenAI) were used for limited drafting and editing of the manuscript. The research questions, problem formulation, theorem statements, proof strategies, experimental design, and interpretation of results were developed by the authors. The authors reviewed and verified all AI-assisted content and take responsibility for the final manuscript and accompanying artifacts.

Reproducibility statement

Reproducibility details are provided in the paper and appendices. Section 3 describes the architectures, training objective and graph data, and Section 6 describes the Countdown and maze tasks and the retry procedure. Appendix B.1 gives the training and evaluation protocols, Appendix B.2 details the mechanistic analyses, and Appendices B.3 and B.4 report additional experiments, controls and method comparisons. Appendix A provides the explicit Transformer construction and proofs. We will release the code publicly.

We also checked auxiliary steps in Lean 4 using the Mathlib library: the ReLU identity (2) and its sum over nodes, the bounds on the errors caused by finite attention scores, the bounds on softmax probabilities, and the counting inequality used in Theorem 3. The theorem concerns positions after at least one generated transition and before the current node equals the target. It does not specify the initial prediction of ss from “s​ts\ t” or the end-of-line prediction after reaching tt. At the first step, k=0k=0 and the input is “s​t​ss\ t\ s”. Detection is unchanged. After a valid transition, or at the first step, if no out-neighbour of the current node is observed to reach tt, the model outputs with probability at least 1−ε1-\varepsilon an out-neighbour of the current node or a node observed to reach tt, provided this set is nonempty. ∎

A.2 Lower Bound on FFN Width

We prove Theorem 3 in the setting of §4.3: the FFN input is xp,i,t=ep⊕ei⊕et∈ℝ3​nx_{p,i,t}=e_{p}\oplus e_{i}\oplus e_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{3n} with n=|V|n=|V|, and the FFN’s contribution to the abort logit is (3).

Scalar form and fixed target.

With W1(p),W1(i),W1(t)W_{1}^{(p)},W_{1}^{(i)},W_{1}^{(t)} the row blocks of W1W_{1} from §4.3, let wh=(W2WU[:,x])[h]w_{h}=\bigl(W_{2}\,W^{U}[:,\texttt{x}]\bigr)[h] be the weight with which unit hh enters the abort logit and β=b2WU[:,x]\beta=b_{2}\,W^{U}[:,\texttt{x}]. Ft0​(p,i):=zxFFN​(p,i,t0)=β+∑h=1rwh​ReLU⁡(W1(p)​[p,h]+W1(i)​[i,h]+bh′).F_{t_{0}}(p,i):=z_{\texttt{x}}^{\mathrm{FFN}}(p,i,t_{0})=\beta+\sum_{h=1}^{r}w_{h}\operatorname{ReLU}\bigl(W_{1}^{(p)}[p,h]+W_{1}^{(i)}[i,h]+b^{\prime}_{h}\bigr). (7)

Let 𝒢r\mathcal{G}_{r} be the class of Boolean functions 𝟏[Ft0(p,i)>0]\mathbf{1}[F_{t_{0}}(p,i)>0] on V×VV\times V, with W1(p),W1(i)∈ℝn×rW_{1}^{(p)},W_{1}^{(i)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r}, b′,w∈ℝrb^{\prime},w\in\mathbb{R}^{r} and β∈ℝ\beta\in\mathbb{R} arbitrary. An FFN that is correct for every target must also be correct for this fixed target. Its decision rule belongs to 𝒢r\mathcal{G}_{r}, so a lower bound for this class also applies when the FFN receives the target as an input.

Theorem 3.

Suppose that a width-rr one-hidden-layer ReLU FFN receives the previous node pp, current node ii, and target tt as the input ep⊕ei⊕ete_{p}\oplus e_{i}\oplus e_{t}. If, for every DAG on |V||V| nodes, there exist FFN parameters for which the sign of zxFFN​(p,i,t)z_{\texttt{x}}^{\mathrm{FFN}}(p,i,t) correctly determines whether (p,i)∈E(p,i)\in E for every p,i,t∈Vp,i,t\in V, then r=Ω⁡(|V|/log2⁡|V|)r=\Omega\bigl(|V|/\log^{2}|V|\bigr).

Proof.

Fix t0t_{0} and let 𝒢r\mathcal{G}_{r} be the class defined above. The proof compares how many labellings of V×VV\times V the class 𝒢r\mathcal{G}_{r} can induce with how many it must induce.

Step 1: number of parameters. A member of 𝒢r\mathcal{G}_{r} is specified by the 2​n​r2nr entries of W1(p)W_{1}^{(p)} and W1(i)W_{1}^{(i)}, the rr entries each of b′b^{\prime} and ww, and β\beta. Hence

P=r⁡(2​n+2)+1≤4​r​n(n≥2,r≥1),P=r(2n+2)+1\leq 4rn\qquad(n\geq 2,\ r\geq 1),

since r⁡(2​n+2)+1≤4​r​nr(2n+2)+1\leq 4rn is equivalent to 1≤r⁡(2​n−2)1\leq r(2n-2).

Step 2: VC dimension. 𝒢r\mathcal{G}_{r} contains the binary decisions obtained by thresholding a one-hidden-layer ReLU network with PP real parameters, evaluated on the finite input set {ep⊕ei}⊂ℝ2​n\{e_{p}\oplus e_{i}\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{2n}. The Vapnik–Chervonenkis (VC) dimension is the largest number of inputs on which a function class can realise every binary labelling. The VC dimension of the sign of a piecewise-linear network with PP parameters and a constant number of layers is at most C​P​log⁡PC\,P\log P for an absolute constant CC (Bartlett et al., 2019); restricting the domain cannot increase it. By Step 1 and monotonicity of P​log⁡PP\log P,

D:=VCdim⁡(𝒢r)≤C​P​log⁡P≤4​C​r​n​log⁡(4​r​n).D:=\operatorname{VCdim}(\mathcal{G}_{r})\leq C\,P\log P\leq 4C\,rn\log(4rn). (8)

Step 3: how many labellings 𝒢r\mathcal{G}_{r} can induce. The domain V×VV\times V has m=n2m=n^{2} points. By the Sauer–Shelah lemma, a class of VC dimension DD induces at most ∑k=0D(mk)≤(m+1)D\sum_{k=0}^{D}\binom{m}{k}\leq(m+1)^{D} distinct labellings of an mm-point set. Thus the number induced by 𝒢r\mathcal{G}_{r} on V×VV\times V satisfies

|𝒢r|≤(n2+1)D.\bigl|\mathcal{G}_{r}\bigr|\leq(n^{2}+1)^{D}. (9)

Step 4: how many labellings it must induce. Fix the node ordering 1,…,n1,\dots,n and consider the graphs whose edges all go from a smaller index to a larger index. Every subset of the (n2)\binom{n}{2} pairs {(p,i):p<i}\{(p,i):p<i\} is such a graph, and each is a DAG because its edges follow a fixed topological order. Distinct subsets have distinct adjacency matrices, so there are 2(n2)=2n⁡(n−1)/22^{\binom{n}{2}}=2^{n(n-1)/2} distinct adjacency relations. By hypothesis each of these DAGs is detected by some FFN, and by the fixed-target reduction the restriction of that FFN’s decision rule to t=t0t=t_{0} is a member of 𝒢r\mathcal{G}_{r} whose labelling of V×VV\times V is the indicator of the non-edges of that DAG. Distinct DAGs give distinct labellings, so

|𝒢r|≥2n⁡(n−1)/2.\bigl|\mathcal{G}_{r}\bigr|\geq 2^{n(n-1)/2}. (10)

Conclusion. Combining (9) and (10) and taking base-two logarithms,

D≥n⁡(n−1)2​log2⁡(n2+1)=Ω⁡(n2log⁡n).D\geq\frac{n(n-1)}{2\log_{2}(n^{2}+1)}=\Omega\!\left(\frac{n^{2}}{\log n}\right).

With (8) this gives r​n​log⁡(4​r​n)=Ω⁡(n2/log⁡n)rn\log(4rn)=\Omega(n^{2}/\log n), that is,

r​log⁡(4​r​n)=Ω⁡(nlog⁡n).r\log(4rn)=\Omega\!\left(\frac{n}{\log n}\right).

If r>nr>n, the claimed asymptotic lower bound already holds. Otherwise r≤nr\leq n, so log⁡(4​r​n)≤log⁡(4​n2)=O⁡(log⁡n)\log(4rn)\leq\log(4n^{2})=O(\log n), and dividing the display by log⁡(4​r​n)\log(4rn) gives r=Ω⁡(n/log2⁡n)r=\Omega(n/\log^{2}n). In either case r=Ω⁡(|V|/log2⁡|V|)r=\Omega\bigl(|V|/\log^{2}|V|\bigr). ∎

Matching upper bound.

The detector of Theorem 2 lies in this class with r=|V|r=|V|. Setting W1(p)​[p,v]=A(p,v)trueW_{1}^{(p)}[p,v]=A^{\mathrm{true}}_{(p,v)}, W1(i)[i,v]=𝟏[i=v]W_{1}^{(i)}[i,v]=\mathbf{1}[i=v], W1(t)=0W_{1}^{(t)}=0, b1​[v]=−1b_{1}[v]=-1, wv=−6​cw_{v}=-6c and β=3​c\beta=3c, unit vv computes (2) and zxFFN​(p,i,t)=3​c−6​c​A(p,i)truez_{\texttt{x}}^{\mathrm{FFN}}(p,i,t)=3c-6c\,A^{\mathrm{true}}_{(p,i)}, which is positive exactly on non-edges. In the Transformer of Appendix A.1 the map ep↦Atrue(p,:)e_{p}\mapsto A^{\mathrm{true}}_{(p,:)} is supplied by head 2; here it is absorbed into W1(p)W_{1}^{(p)}. Appendix B Experimental Details and Extended Results

B.1 Setup and Evaluation Details

Training objective.

The trained models apply layer normalisation before attention, before the FFN and before unembedding. Let 𝒟\mathcal{D} be the training set. For each sequence u=(u1,…,uN)u=(u_{1},\dots,u_{N}), the supervision mask μ∈{0,1}N\mu\in\{0,1\}^{N} marks which tokens receive a loss:

ℒ(𝒟)=−∑u∈𝒟∑q=1N−1μq+1logPr[uq+1∣u1:q].\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{D})\;=\;-\sum_{u\in\mathcal{D}}\sum_{q=1}^{N-1}\mu_{q+1}\,\log\Pr\!\left[u_{q+1}\mid u_{1:q}\right]. (11)

Correct trajectories supervise every non-padding next token after the first; an error trajectory (s,t,s,u1,…,uk,w,x)(s,\ t,\ s,\ u_{1},\dots,u_{k},\ w,\ \texttt{x}), with u0=su_{0}=s when k=0k=0, supervises only the final x. Minibatch losses are averaged over supervised labels.

Graph data.

The distinct non-edges used in the error trajectories cover 8282–93%93\% of all non-edges, more at larger nn. The +x+\texttt{x} data sets range from 67,00067{,}000 sequences (2.12.1 million padded token slots) at n=100n=100 to 2.492.49 million sequences (79.679.6 million slots) at n=500n=500. On the n=300n=300 data, 37.4±0.3%37.4\pm 0.3\% of the positions supervised to emit x also end at a node from which the target is unreachable, so the abort label is not a dead-end label. A correct trajectory carries 6.16.1 supervised labels on average at n=100n=100 and 8.18.1 at n=500n=500, whereas an error trajectory carries one; with half of each +x+\texttt{x} batch made of error trajectories, the +x+\texttt{x} model sees 0.50×0.50\times the baseline’s correct trajectories per update in expectation (measured at n=100n=100, 300300 and 500500). This is a ratio of trajectory counts, not a ratio of loss weights. Appendix B.3 doubles +x+\texttt{x} updates to match correct-trajectory exposure.

Output classification.

Prompted with s t, the model emits tokens until end-of-line or, for a +x+\texttt{x} model, the abort token, subject to the generation-length limit. An output is valid if it is a path from ss to tt containing only graph edges, and invalid otherwise. Invalid outputs are classified in the evaluator’s order as abort (it contains x), syntax (too few node tokens), wrong-end (v0≠sv_{0}\neq s or vL≠tv_{L}\neq t for the output v0,…,vLv_{0},\dots,v_{L}) or non-edge (correct endpoints but some (vq−1,vq)∉E(v_{q-1},v_{q})\notin E). Every output containing x counts as abort, whether or not the abort is justified, including one whose last transition before x is a non-edge; a wrong-end output may also contain a non-edge.

Evaluation, abort precision and selective accuracy.

Harness results use 3,0003{,}000 instances drawn with replacement from the held-out set, with K=100K=100, in all three domains of §6. Graph single-shot validity is evaluated on every held-out instance, the Countdown single-shot results use the same 3,0003{,}000 instances as the harness, and the maze results average two independent sampling runs per maze. An abort emitted after a prefix y1:ky_{1:k} is

justified⇔no completion of y1:k is a valid output for the instance,\textsf{justified}\iff\text{no completion of }y_{1:k}\text{ is a valid output for the instance}, (12)

and abort precision is the fraction of emitted aborts that are justified. In the graph domain a prefix admits a valid completion exactly when it starts at ss, follows edges and ends at a node that can reach tt, which we check exhaustively on GG. For the fitted models of Appendix B.2, we instead report the fraction of total abort probability assigned to prefixes that admit a valid completion.

We also compare aborting with rejecting outputs that have low mean token log-probability. Coverage is the fraction of instances whose outputs are retained; selective accuracy is the fraction of those retained outputs that are valid. For +x+\texttt{x}, we retain every non-aborting output. For the baseline, we discard the lowest-scoring outputs until the same fraction is retained. These measurements use one draw per instance, without retry.

Compute.

Graph models are trained in bfloat16 on one NVIDIA H200 GPU. The two d=120d{=}120 architectures have the same 0.20.2 million parameters, because increasing the head count divides the same embedding size among more heads; the d=384d=384 model has about 1.91.9 million.

B.2 Additional Mechanistic Results

Interventions on previous-node attention and the FFN.

The interventions of §5.1 use the 1/2/3841/2/384 +x+\texttt{x} models of six n=300n=300 graphs: the five evaluation seeds and the graph of Figure 7. For each graph, we take 2,0002{,}000 held-out valid prefixes for which a previous-node swap exists, append a non-successor node and measure P⁡(x)P(\texttt{x}) at the next position. Removing attention to a position sets its weight at the final query to zero and renormalises the remaining weights; the main head is the head with more previous-node attention on invalid prefixes. Removing the FFN output sets it to zero before the residual addition. Means ±\pm s.e. are over graphs.

Table 1 adds controls and the full sample to Table 2. On target-reachable prefixes, removing target or current-node attention leaves P⁡(x)P(\texttt{x}) at 0.9110.911 or 0.9970.997, and removing previous-node attention in the other head leaves it at 0.8610.861, so the effect is specific to previous-node attention, mostly in the main head. On the other 81.7±0.3%81.7\pm 0.3\% of prefixes the appended node cannot reach the target, so an abort remains justified after the swap; the model still aborts there with mean probability 0.72±0.010.72\pm 0.01, which keeps the all-prefix column near 0.60.6. On valid prefixes, removing previous-node attention in both heads makes P⁡(x)>0.5P(\texttt{x})>0.5 on only 2.4±0.7%2.4\pm 0.7\% of prefixes.

As a consistency check, we also copy the complete attention output at the final position between the invalid and swapped prefixes. Because the model has only one layer, the final token ww and its positional embedding are identical in the two prefixes, and the attention output is the only component at that position that depends on the earlier tokens before the FFN. The patched prefix therefore gives the same abort decision as the corresponding swapped input. On target-reachable prefixes, copying the swapped prefix’s attention output into the invalid prefix gives P⁡(x)=0.001P(\texttt{x})=0.001, as does the previous-node swap itself (Table 1). This checks the intervention implementation rather than providing an independent test of the mechanism.

Direct logit attribution.

At the final position, write the residual stream before the final layer normalisation as H=Y+MH=Y+M, where Y=X+MHA⁡(LN1⁡(X))Y=X+\operatorname{MHA}(\operatorname{LN}_{1}(X)) is the stream entering the FFN and MM is the FFN output, as in §5.2. With wxw_{\texttt{x}} the abort column of WUW^{U} and gg the scale of the final layer normalisation, which has no bias, the abort logit is wx⊤​[g⊙(H−mean⁡(H))/std⁡(H)]w_{\texttt{x}}^{\top}\bigl[g\odot(H-\operatorname{mean}(H))/\operatorname{std}(H)\bigr], where std⁡(H)\operatorname{std}(H) includes the numerical stabiliser. Centring is linear and std⁡(H)\operatorname{std}(H) is a single scalar for the forward pass, so the logit splits exactly into zxY+zxMz^{Y}_{\texttt{x}}+z^{M}_{\texttt{x}} with

zxC=wx⊤​[g⊙C−mean⁡(C)std⁡(H)],C∈{Y,M}.z^{C}_{\texttt{x}}=w_{\texttt{x}}^{\top}\Bigl[g\odot\frac{C-\operatorname{mean}(C)}{\operatorname{std}(H)}\Bigr],\qquad C\in\{Y,M\}.

For the abort margin, replace wxw_{\texttt{x}} by wx−wv∗w_{\texttt{x}}-w_{v^{*}}, where v∗v^{*} is the node with the highest logit on that prefix. The trained FFN has no output bias, so M=∑hαhW2[h,:]M=\sum_{h}\alpha_{h}W_{2}[h,:] with αh\alpha_{h} the activation of unit hh, and the same formula gives each unit’s contribution. Table 2 reports these quantities on the prefixes of Table 1.

The pre-FFN contribution stays near −1-1 in all four conditions, including the valid continuation and the target-unreachable invalid prefixes. On valid prefixes the FFN’s contribution to the abort logit is positive on 90%90\% of prefixes, while its margin contribution is −8.1-8.1: it raises the highest node logit more than the abort logit. This polarity is the reverse of the construction in Appendix A.1, where a constant abort bias is cancelled by units that fire after a valid transition. In the trained models the ten units with the most negative contributions on valid prefixes sum to only −1.1±0.1-1.1\pm 0.1 there, and to +8.4±1.7+8.4\pm 1.7 on invalid prefixes. A detection unit ReLU(𝟏[i=v]−A(p,v)true)=𝟏[i=v](1−A(p,v)true)\mathrm{ReLU}(\mathbf{1}[i=v]-A^{\mathrm{true}}_{(p,v)})=\mathbf{1}[i=v](1-A^{\mathrm{true}}_{(p,v)}), which fires after an invalid transition, implements the same check with the same width when its output weight is +6​c+6c and the abort bias is −3​c-3c. Most of the FFN contribution on invalid prefixes comes from a small set of units: 1616 units exceed 0.250.25 when the target remains reachable (2222 when it does not), the ten largest carry 6363–87%87\% of the FFN contribution, and 1616 (3131) units reach 90%90\% of it.

Additive fits.

Could the supervised abort decision be reproduced by separate additive contributions of the previous node pp, current node ii and target tt? We fit, to the supervised training labels of the n=300n=300 graph of Figure 7 rather than to the trained model, the additive-logit model

z⁡(ℓ)=W(i,ℓ)M+W(t,ℓ)V+W(p,ℓ)P,z(\ell)\;=\;W^{M}_{(i,\ell)}+W^{V}_{(t,\ell)}+W^{P}_{(p,\ell)}, (13)

where ℓ\ell is a candidate output token and WM,WV,WP∈ℝ|V|×MW^{M},W^{V},W^{P}\in\mathbb{R}^{|V|\times M} are free matrices: a linear readout of three one-hot inputs with no term depending jointly on pp and ii. This is the form computed by a fixed-attention Transformer in which two heads copy the target and previous-node representations, the residual supplies the current node, and the remaining maps are linear. With WP=0W^{P}=0 it is the additive model of Wang et al. (2024), which gives every prefix with the same (i,t)(i,t) the same next-token distribution. The abort probability of (13) is a softmax over all candidate logits rather than a thresholded additive score, so Proposition 1 does not apply directly; we test the fit empirically.

The fit uses every supervised position whose prefix ends at u0=su_{0}=s or at a later node, 2,784,4402{,}784{,}440 positions grouped by (p,i,t)(p,i,t): 425,002425{,}002 follow an invalid transition, and the rest come from correct trajectories and all admit a valid completion. The logits are linear in the fitted matrices, so the objective is convex; Adam followed by L-BFGS reaches ‖∇ℒ¯‖∞≤6.3×10−7\|\nabla\overline{\mathcal{L}}\|_{\infty}\leq 6.3\times 10^{-7} for the loss averaged over these positions. Let 𝒮\mathcal{S} be the multiset of these prefixes and 𝒞⊆𝒮\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathcal{S} those admitting a valid completion (source-only prefixes, for which the fit sets p=i=sp=i=s, belong to 𝒞\mathcal{C}). The unjustified-abort mass fraction ∑y∈𝒞P⁡(x∣y)/∑y∈𝒮P⁡(x∣y)\sum_{y\in\mathcal{C}}P(\texttt{x}\mid y)/\sum_{y\in\mathcal{S}}P(\texttt{x}\mid y) is the share of total abort probability placed on prefixes that could still be completed correctly; we also report the mean P⁡(x∣y)P(\texttt{x}\mid y) over ℐ=𝒮∖𝒞\mathcal{I}=\mathcal{S}\setminus\mathcal{C}. For the fit these two percentages sum to 100%100\%, because at a stationary point of the objective the total abort probability equals the number of abort labels; this need not hold for the trained Transformer.

The fit also assigns about 8%8\% abort probability after a valid transition, against 0.01%0.01\% for the trained model (Table 3). Separate additive contributions therefore do not reproduce the learned rejection quality even with the previous node available.

Planning representations and attention heads.

We examine planning information with two probes adapted from Wang et al. (2024). Let W¯V:=[WV(1)​∣⋯∣​WV(H)]​WA\overline{W}_{V}:=[W_{V}^{(1)}\mid\cdots\mid W_{V}^{(H)}]W^{A} be the value map of the attention layer when both heads place all their attention on the target position, and let eve_{v} be the one-hot vector of node vv. The probes are

W(i,ℓ)M′=[(FFN⁡(ei⊤​Wt)+ei⊤​Wt)​WU]ℓ,W(t,ℓ)V′=[(ot+FFN⁡(ot))​WU]ℓ,W^{M^{\prime}}_{(i,\ell)}=\bigl[(\mathrm{FFN}(e_{i}^{\top}W_{t})+e_{i}^{\top}W_{t})W^{U}\bigr]_{\ell},\qquad W^{V^{\prime}}_{(t,\ell)}=\bigl[(o_{t}+\mathrm{FFN}(o_{t}))W^{U}\bigr]_{\ell},

with ot=et⊤​Wt​W¯Vo_{t}=e_{t}^{\top}W_{t}\overline{W}_{V}. The first probe passes the current-node embedding through the FFN with its residual connection and probes adjacency information associated with the current node; the second does the same for the target embedding after the value map and probes reachability information associated with the target. Here FFN is the trained GELU map, and positional embeddings and layer normalisations are omitted, following Wang et al. (2024). Because the FFN is nonlinear, the probes are diagnostics of the learned weights, not decompositions of the actual logits; primes distinguish them from the fitted matrices of (13).

At the end of training, the WM′W^{M^{\prime}} edge/non-edge gap of the +x+\texttt{x} models is slightly above the baselines’ at both sizes, 0.1190.119 against 0.1100.110 at d=120d{=}120 and 0.2200.220 against 0.2020.202 at d=384d{=}384 (Figure 6a). The gap compares edges and non-edges among forward pairs i<vi<v in the graph’s node ordering. This is consistent with error trajectories providing additional adjacency supervision.

For reachability, a pair (t,u)(t,u) is observed reachable if R(t,u)obs=1R^{\mathrm{obs}}_{(t,u)}=1, with RobsR^{\mathrm{obs}} as in Remark 1, unobserved reachable if R(t,u)true=1R^{\mathrm{true}}_{(t,u)}=1 but R(t,u)obs=0R^{\mathrm{obs}}_{(t,u)}=0, and unreachable if R(t,u)true=0R^{\mathrm{true}}_{(t,u)}=0. Figure 6b shows mean WV′W^{V^{\prime}} values over u<tu<t for these groups in the two-head baseline models. The observed-reachable minus unobserved-reachable gap is positive across all three architectures and five graph sizes, and the unobserved-reachable minus unreachable gap is larger in 1313 of these 1515 configurations, so WV′W^{V^{\prime}} carries some information about true reachability beyond the observed pairs, with additional separation for observed pairs.

At 1/2/3841/2/384 one head attends to the target and the other to the current position in all five seeds, for both baseline and +x+\texttt{x} models (Figure 7); which head takes which role varies between runs.

B.3 Additional Graph Planning Results

Single-shot validity and model size.

Abort supervision leaves single-shot validity unchanged at n=100n=100 for all three architectures. It lowers it for the d=120d{=}120 models by 2.0±0.22.0\pm 0.2 and 2.5±0.32.5\pm 0.3 percentage points at n=200n=200 (one and two heads) and by 11.6±0.311.6\pm 0.3 and 11.3±0.411.3\pm 0.4 points at n=500n=500; at d=384d{=}384 the change is within the error bars at n=200n=200 and between −0.9±0.1-0.9\pm 0.1 and −2.8±0.0-2.8\pm 0.0 points from n=300n=300 on (Figure 3a). The cost is larger for the d=120d{=}120 models, whose abort precision is also lower (6868–94%94\%, against 9494–99%99\% at d=384d{=}384). The difference is associated with embedding size rather than head count: 1/2/1201/2/120 tracks 1/1/1201/1/120 within about one point at the same parameter count, which is why §5 uses the two-head models.

Matched correct-trajectory supervision.

Because half of the trajectories in a +x+\texttt{x} batch carry a single label, the +x+\texttt{x} model receives half the baseline’s correct-trajectory supervision per update (§B.1). We therefore also train both 1/2/3841/2/384 models for 20,00020{,}000 updates on the n=300n=300 graph of Figure 7, after which the +x+\texttt{x} model has seen the correct-trajectory supervision the baseline receives in 10,00010{,}000. Harness validity in percent on that graph:

updates baseline ++ retry +x+\texttt{x} ++ retry gain
10,00010{,}000 (the setting used throughout) 97.697.6 99.699.6 +2.0+2.0
20,00020{,}000 96.996.9 99.699.6 +2.7+2.7

At matched correct-trajectory exposure, the 20,00020{,}000-update +x+\texttt{x} model exceeds the 10,00010{,}000-update baseline by 2.02.0 percentage points. The longer-trained baseline is slightly worse, its invalid-transition rate rising from 2.4%2.4\% to 3.1%3.1\%.

B.4 Additional Tasks and Method Comparisons

A pretrained model on Blocksworld.

The three domains above use one-layer models trained from scratch. We also evaluate abort supervision on a pretrained language model, Qwen3-0.6B-Base, on Blocksworld with 88 or 99 blocks. A move takes an uncovered block and places it on the table or on another uncovered block. The prompt gives the initial and goal configurations as stacks; the model writes one move per line (move A onto B, move A onto table) and then done, and never restates the state. Each instance is an initial–goal pair whose shortest solution, found by breadth-first search from the goal, has 44–1515 moves. Of 300300 goals (150150 per block count), 255255 are training goals with 4040 initial states each, giving 10,20010{,}200 plans; 4545 are held-out goals with 6060 initial states each, and evaluation uses 2,0002{,}000 of these 2,7002{,}700 instances. Error trajectories take a valid prefix of a training plan, append one invalid move (moving a buried block, moving onto a buried block, or a no-op) and a new token <|abort|> playing the role of x, with the loss on that token only; ρ=8\rho=8. Both models are fine-tuned for 33 epochs (learning rate 2×10−52\times 10^{-5}, batch size 6464) on one NVIDIA A100 GPU; because the +x+\texttt{x} training set is nine times as large, it receives nine times as many updates, and a second baseline trained for 2727 epochs matches its update count. The harness draws at most K=10K=10 plans per instance at temperature 11 and accepts the first that does not abort and ends with done; it does not check moves or the final state, and validity is scored by simulation.

Retrying on the abort raises harness validity from 70.4±0.9%70.4\pm 0.9\% to 93.3±0.3%93.3\pm 0.3\%, a gain of +22.9±1.0+22.9\pm 1.0 percentage points at 1.101.10 draws per instance, and of +6.8±0.6+6.8\pm 0.6 points over the baseline trained for the same number of updates. Illegal moves account for most invalid outputs in every arm: they appear in 26.7%26.7\% of the outputs returned by the baseline harness, 8.9%8.9\% for the matched-steps baseline and 5.9%5.9\% for the +x+\texttt{x} harness (Figure 8b). At the coverage of the +x+\texttt{x} model, 93.1%93.1\% of instances, its selective accuracy is 94.1%94.1\%, against 75.1%75.1\% for a mean-log-probability threshold on the baseline and 88.4%88.4\% on the matched-steps baseline.

Self-Backtracking on Countdown.

We adapt Self-Backtracking (Yang et al., 2026) to the same error trajectories as +x+\texttt{x}. Its loss supervises the correct prefix and a backtrack token after the invalid step, masking only that step. Training otherwise matches the Countdown runs of §6: the same 1/2/3841/2/384 model, split, error trajectories at ρ=1\rho=1, 10,00010{,}000 updates, optimiser and five seeds, and the backtrack token uses the same vocabulary entry as the abort token. The baseline and +x+\texttt{x} models are the ρ=1\rho=1 models of §6, evaluated on the same 3,0003{,}000 test instances with fresh samples, so their single-shot validity differs slightly from the values there.

At inference, Self-Backtracking first samples NN trajectories and keeps completed outputs without a backtrack token as candidates. For outputs that emit the token, it removes the last equation and selects up to ⌊N⌋\lfloor\sqrt{N}\rfloor distinct shortened prefixes. It then samples NN continuations from each selected prefix. This is one round of backtracking, denoted b=1b=1. The likelihood selection rule returns the candidate with the highest mean token log-probability. We also evaluate the harness rule of §6, which selects the first candidate whose last written value is the target.

For each instance, the output-token count used by Self-Backtracking at a given NN sets a hard budget for baseline and +x+\texttt{x} restart. A final restart draw that would exceed this budget is truncated and discarded. We also exchange the inference procedures to separate their effect from the training loss: the Self-Backtracking model uses restart under the same token budget, and the +x+\texttt{x} model uses backtracking with the same NN. The latter has similar, but not identical, token counts. All combinations are evaluated under both selection rules; the resource comparison concerns generated output tokens, not wall-clock time.

Figure 9 shows the results. Single-shot validity rises by +2.1±0.5+2.1\pm 0.5 percentage points for +x+\texttt{x} and by +0.3±0.7+0.3\pm 0.7 for Self-Backtracking. Under the likelihood rule at N=32N=32 (about 470470 tokens per instance) the baseline reaches 43.1±0.8%43.1\pm 0.8\%, Self-Backtracking 49.3±0.7%49.3\pm 0.7\% and +x+\texttt{x} 51.5±0.8%51.5\pm 0.8\%. The paired difference between +x+\texttt{x} and Self-Backtracking is +2.0+2.0 to +2.2+2.2 points at every budget from N=4N=4 on and positive on every seed, and +1.7+1.7 to +2.3+2.3 points under the harness rule (+0.7±0.7+0.7\pm 0.7 and +0.8±0.9+0.8\pm 0.9 at N=2N=2). Exchanging inference procedures suggests that the loss accounts for most of the difference in this setting: at N=32N=32, the +x+\texttt{x} model with backtracking reaches 51.6±0.9%51.6\pm 0.9\%, and the Self-Backtracking model with restart reaches 49.3±0.7%49.3\pm 0.7\%, close to their results with the original procedures. One round of backtracking adds 0.30.3 to 1.61.6 points over selecting from the same initial samples without backtracking (b=0b=0). We also evaluate the released-code variant, which expands only one shortened prefix and does not expand it if no equations remain, and a temperature-0.70.7 variant. Both are shown in the figure and perform at or below the ⌊N⌋\lfloor\sqrt{N}\rfloor rule at temperature 11 under likelihood selection.
